## Introduction

In class we learnt about four classifiers: **LDA**, **QDA**, **naive Bayes**, and
**k-nearest neighbors**. Three of them are generative Gaussian methods that
differ only in what they assume about the covariance; k-NN is the
non-parametric alternative. This lab fits all four to the same medical
diagnosis problem and compares them the way the slides told us to — with the
confusion matrix, sensitivity, specificity, and the ROC curve.

Every code cell runs live in your browser via webR — no local R install
needed. Edit any cell and re-run it. Packages and data load once when the page
opens; give it a few seconds on first load. **The k-NN cross-validation step is
the heaviest cell and may take a little longer.**

## A note on `caret`

Following [Lab 3](../../03-regression-1/code/class3_lab1.html), every model
goes through `caret::train()` with **one shared interface**. We change the
`method` argument and nothing else: `"lda"`, `"qda"`, `"nb"`, `"knn"`. The same
cross-validation settings and the same centering/scaling apply to all four, so
a difference in the results is a difference between the *methods*, not between
how we called them.

## The data: Wisconsin breast tumors

The Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer (WDBC) dataset records 569 tumors from
fine-needle-aspirate images. Each tumor is labeled **Benign** or **Malignant**
— a binary outcome, so the ROC curve and AUC work directly. Ten features are
measured (radius, texture, smoothness, and so on); for each feature the data
gives its mean, standard error, and "worst" value across the image, for 30
columns in all.

```{webr}
library(dplyr)

wdbc <- read.csv("data/wdbc.csv") |>
  mutate(diagnosis = factor(diagnosis, levels = c("B", "M"),
                            labels = c("Benign", "Malignant")))

table(wdbc$diagnosis)
```

About 63% of the tumors are benign and 37% malignant — imbalanced, but not
severely. Keep that split in mind: a classifier that called *everything* benign
would already be 63% accurate while catching zero cancers (so accuracy alone will
not be enough to track performance, we need to look at *other* metrics).

### Choosing the features

The full 30 features separate the two classes almost perfectly (test AUC near
0.98 - take my word for it although you are free to check :)). Every method would look great and
we would learn nothing about their differences; so we deliberately keep a
harder subset: **four features, each in its mean and standard-error form**.

```{webr}
soft <- c("texture_mean", "smoothness_mean", "symmetry_mean", "fractal_dim_mean",
          "texture_se",   "smoothness_se",   "symmetry_se",   "fractal_dim_se")

dat <- wdbc[, c("diagnosis", soft)]
head(dat)
```

### Train / test split

```{webr}
library(caret)

set.seed(2155)
idx <- createDataPartition(dat$diagnosis, p = 0.75, list = FALSE)
train_data <- dat[idx, ]
test_data  <- dat[-idx, ]

c(train = nrow(train_data), test = nrow(test_data))
```

`createDataPartition` keeps the benign/malignant ratio the same in both parts.
We tune and fit on the 427 training tumors and judge every model on the same
142 held-out test tumors.

## Fitting the four models

The shared control object below asks for 10-fold cross-validation and, because
we will want predicted probabilities for the ROC curve, class probabilities.

```{webr}
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10, classProbs = TRUE)
```

### LDA and QDA

LDA assumes a single shared covariance matrix across classes (linear
boundary); QDA gives each class its own (quadratic boundary). Same call, one
argument apart.

```{webr}
library(MASS)

set.seed(2155)
lda_model <- train(diagnosis ~ ., data = train_data, method = "lda",
                   trControl = ctrl, preProcess = c("center", "scale"))

set.seed(2155)
qda_model <- train(diagnosis ~ ., data = train_data, method = "qda",
                   trControl = ctrl, preProcess = c("center", "scale"))
```

### Naive Bayes

Naive Bayes keeps the generative recipe but assumes the features are
independent within each class — a *diagonal* covariance. Here we use the
Gaussian version (`usekernel = FALSE`), matching the density in the slides (but remember, Naive Bayes is the ONLY generative model that allows for mixed data types!)

The `suppressWarnings()` wrapper hides a harmless "numerical 0 probability"
message: on a few outlying tumors the Gaussian density underflows to zero. It
does not affect the fit. Note that **technically** Naive Bayes could have other distributions to support feature space as well!

```{webr}
library(klaR)

set.seed(2155)
nb_model <- suppressWarnings(
  train(diagnosis ~ ., data = train_data, method = "nb",
        trControl = ctrl, preProcess = c("center", "scale"),
        tuneGrid = expand.grid(fL = 0, usekernel = FALSE, adjust = 1))
)
```

### k-Nearest Neighbors

k-NN is non-parametric — no distribution assumed. We let cross-validation pick
`k` from the odd numbers 1 to 25. This is the heaviest cell; give it a moment.

```{webr}
set.seed(2155)
knn_model <- train(diagnosis ~ ., data = train_data, method = "knn",
                   trControl = ctrl, preProcess = c("center", "scale"),
                   tuneGrid = expand.grid(k = seq(1, 25, by = 2)))

knn_model$bestTune
```

Cross-validation chooses **k = 15** — not k = 1. That matches the slide's
warning: a very small `k` overfits (low bias, high variance), so CV pulls us
toward a smoother boundary.

## Evaluating on the test set

The confusion matrix from the slides, in code. We set `positive = "Malignant"`
because catching cancer is the outcome we care about, so **sensitivity** =
"of the true malignant tumors, how many did we catch?" and **specificity** =
"of the true benign tumors, how many did we correctly clear?"

```{webr}
lda_preds <- predict(lda_model, test_data)
confusionMatrix(lda_preds, test_data$diagnosis, positive = "Malignant")
```

Read the output against the slides: **Accuracy** is the overall proportion
correct, **Sensitivity** and **Specificity** are the two class-wise rates, and
Youden's J = Sensitivity + Specificity − 1 summarizes both in one number.

Now the other three:

```{webr}
qda_preds <- predict(qda_model, test_data)
confusionMatrix(qda_preds, test_data$diagnosis, positive = "Malignant")
```

```{webr}
nb_preds <- suppressWarnings(predict(nb_model, test_data))
confusionMatrix(nb_preds, test_data$diagnosis, positive = "Malignant")
```

```{webr}
knn_preds <- predict(knn_model, test_data)
confusionMatrix(knn_preds, test_data$diagnosis, positive = "Malignant")
```

### Putting the four side by side

```{webr}
library(pROC)

summarise_model <- function(model, name) {
  p  <- suppressWarnings(predict(model, test_data))
  cm <- confusionMatrix(p, test_data$diagnosis, positive = "Malignant")
  pr <- suppressWarnings(predict(model, test_data, type = "prob"))[, "Malignant"]
  auc <- as.numeric(auc(roc(test_data$diagnosis, pr,
                            levels = c("Benign", "Malignant"),
                            direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)))
  sens <- cm$byClass["Sensitivity"]; spec <- cm$byClass["Specificity"]
  data.frame(Model = name,
             Accuracy    = round(cm$overall["Accuracy"], 3),
             Sensitivity = round(sens, 3),
             Specificity = round(spec, 3),
             Youden_J    = round(sens + spec - 1, 3),
             AUC         = round(auc, 3),
             row.names = NULL)
}

rbind(
  summarise_model(lda_model, "LDA"),
  summarise_model(qda_model, "QDA"),
  summarise_model(nb_model,  "Naive Bayes"),
  summarise_model(knn_model, "k-NN")
)
```

Three things worth reading off this table:

- **QDA beats LDA** (accuracy 0.838 vs 0.817, Youden's J 0.650 vs 0.593). The
  two classes really do have different covariance structure, so letting each
  class keep its own — the quadratic boundary — pays off. This is the QDA
  lesson from the slides, made concrete.
- **Naive Bayes is the weakest here** (accuracy 0.782). Its independence
  assumption is wrong: these tumor measurements are correlated, and throwing
  the correlations away costs accuracy. A reminder that "naive" is a real
  assumption, not a free lunch.
- **k-NN and QDA tie on accuracy**, but they get there differently: k-NN has
  the highest **specificity** (0.910 — best at clearing benign tumors) while
  QDA has the highest **sensitivity** (0.774 — best at catching cancer). In a
  screening setting a missed malignancy is the costly error, which would push
  you toward QDA even at equal accuracy.

## The ROC curve

Accuracy and the confusion matrix fix a single threshold (predict "Malignant"
when its probability exceeds 0.5). The ROC curve sweeps *every* threshold,
plotting sensitivity against 1 − specificity, and AUC is the area under it.
Let's draw all four on one plot.

```{webr}
library(ggplot2)

roc_df <- function(model, name) {
  pr <- suppressWarnings(predict(model, test_data, type = "prob"))[, "Malignant"]
  r  <- roc(test_data$diagnosis, pr, levels = c("Benign", "Malignant"),
            direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)
  data.frame(fpr = 1 - r$specificities, tpr = r$sensitivities, Model = name)
}

all_roc <- rbind(
  roc_df(lda_model, "LDA"),
  roc_df(qda_model, "QDA"),
  roc_df(nb_model,  "Naive Bayes"),
  roc_df(knn_model, "k-NN")
)

ggplot(all_roc, aes(fpr, tpr, color = Model)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  ggsci::scale_color_aaas() +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "1 − Specificity (False Positive Rate)",
       y = "Sensitivity (True Positive Rate)",
       title = "ROC curves: four classifiers, same test set") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

A curve closer to the top-left corner is better. LDA and k-NN have the highest
AUC (~0.90), even though QDA had the best single-threshold accuracy — a good
illustration that "best classifier" depends on whether you care about one
threshold or the whole range.

## Try it yourself

The comparison above used `set.seed(2155)`. Does the winner depend on that
particular split? Change the seed, re-run the split and the four fits, and see
whether the ranking holds.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_seed
# Change the seed, then re-run this whole cell.
set.seed(______)   # try 1, 7, 2026, your birthday...
idx2 <- createDataPartition(dat$diagnosis, p = 0.75, list = FALSE)
tr2 <- dat[idx2, ]; te2 <- dat[-idx2, ]

set.seed(1); lda2 <- train(diagnosis ~ ., tr2, method = "lda",
                           trControl = ctrl, preProcess = c("center", "scale"))
set.seed(1); qda2 <- train(diagnosis ~ ., tr2, method = "qda",
                           trControl = ctrl, preProcess = c("center", "scale"))

data.frame(
  LDA = mean(predict(lda2, te2) == te2$diagnosis),
  QDA = mean(predict(qda2, te2) == te2$diagnosis)
)
```

Across most splits QDA stays ahead of LDA on this feature set — the covariance
difference is a property of the data, not an accident of one split.

For a second experiment: the lab uses eight features. Add `radius_mean` and
`area_mean` to the `soft` vector near the top, re-run everything, and watch
every model's accuracy jump — those two features carry most of the signal,
which is exactly why we left them out to keep the comparison interesting.

## Things worth remembering

- **One interface, four methods.** `train(method = ...)` let us swap LDA, QDA,
  naive Bayes, and k-NN without relearning four APIs.
- **The covariance assumption is the dial.** LDA (shared) → QDA (per-class) →
  naive Bayes (diagonal) are the same generative idea under different
  restrictions, and on this data QDA's extra flexibility earned its keep while
  naive Bayes' independence assumption cost it.
- **Accuracy is not the whole story.** Sensitivity, specificity, Youden's J,
  and AUC each answer a different question, and for a cancer screen the one
  that matters most is sensitivity.
